title: JSON Web Algorithms (JWA)
summary: This specification registers cryptographic algorithms and identifiers for use with the JSON Web Signature, JSON Web Encryption, and JSON Web Key specifications. It also defines several IANA registries for these identifiers.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7518 defines names and rules for the cryptographic algorithms used by JSON Web Signature, JSON Web Encryption and JSON Web Key. It also defines how keys are represented and how new algorithm names are registered.

subtitle: The named cryptographic algorithms and key formats for JSON Web Signature, Encryption and Key.

tldr.problem: JSON Web Signature, JSON Web Encryption and JSON Web Key need shared names and rules for cryptographic algorithms and key parameters.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7518 defines signature and MAC algorithms, key-management and content-encryption algorithms, key types and parameters, and IANA registries for their identifiers.
tldr.outcome: The specifications can refer to compact identifiers such as HS256, ECDH-ES and A128GCM, with defined operations and implementation requirements. RFC 7518 is updated by RFC 9864.

today: RFC 7518 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 9864. The unit metadata does not list an RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why JWA Defines the Algorithm Names
sections.content:
JSON Web Signature (JWS), JSON Web Encryption (JWE) and JSON Web Key (JWK) use JSON data structures and need identifiers for algorithms and key types. RFC 7518 registers those identifiers and describes the operations each one requires.

Keeping identifiers in a separate specification lets the JWS, JWE and JWK documents remain unchanged as algorithm requirements evolve. The names are short to keep JSON representations compact.

The RFC also defines Base64urlUInt, a way to represent a non-negative integer as the shortest unsigned big-endian octet sequence, then encode it with base64url. Zero is represented as AA.
sections.plainLanguage: JWA defines the names for algorithms used by JWS, JWE and JWK. A separate list lets those names and requirements change without rewriting the format specifications.

sections.title: JWS Signatures and Message Codes
sections.content:
JWS uses a signature or message authentication code to protect its protected header and payload. The RFC defines HMAC with SHA-2 as HS256, HS384 and HS512; RSA signatures using RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 as RS256, RS384 and RS512; ECDSA as ES256, ES384 and ES512; and RSASSA-PSS as PS256, PS384 and PS512.

HS256 is Required, while HS384 and HS512 are Optional. RSA and PSS keys must be at least 2048 bits. ECDSA signatures are encoded as fixed-size R and S values joined together; the result is 64 octets for ES256, 96 for ES384 and 132 for ES512. HMAC verification must use a constant-time comparison.

The none algorithm creates an Unsecured JWS with an empty signature and no integrity protection. Implementations must not accept it by default, and applications should only allow it for specific objects when appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: JWS uses a named algorithm to create a signature or message authentication code for its content. The none option provides no integrity protection and must not be accepted by default.

sections.title: Algorithms for Protecting the JWE Key
sections.content:
JWE encrypts content using a Content Encryption Key (CEK), and the alg header says how the recipient obtains that key. RFC 7518 defines RSA key encryption, AES Key Wrap, direct use of a shared key, ECDH-ES key agreement, AES GCM key wrapping and password-based PBES2 algorithms.

ECDH-ES can derive the CEK directly or derive a key that wraps the CEK. It uses a newly generated ephemeral public key for each key agreement and the Concat KDF with SHA-256. The epk header carries the ephemeral public key; optional apu and apv values provide producer and recipient information.

AES GCM key wrapping uses a 96-bit IV and a 128-bit authentication tag. For PBES2, p2s carries a fresh random salt input of at least 8 octets, and p2c carries the iteration count; a minimum of 1000 iterations is recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: The JWE key-management algorithm tells the recipient how to obtain the key that encrypts the message. The choices include encrypting the key, agreeing on a key, using a shared key or deriving a key from a password.

sections.title: Algorithms for Encrypting JWE Content
sections.content:
The enc header selects how JWE encrypts and integrity-protects its plaintext and authenticates additional data. RFC 7518 defines AES in CBC mode combined with HMAC-SHA-2, and AES in Galois/Counter Mode (GCM). These algorithms produce ciphertext and an authentication tag.

The CBC-HMAC family divides the input key into a MAC key and an encryption key. It encrypts the plaintext with AES-CBC and padding, then computes an HMAC over the additional authenticated data, initialization vector, ciphertext and encoded length of the additional data. The receiver checks the tag before decrypting.

AES GCM requires a 96-bit initialization vector and a 128-bit authentication tag, regardless of the key size. The JWE content-encryption identifiers include A128GCM, A192GCM and A256GCM.
sections.plainLanguage: The content-encryption algorithm encrypts the message and adds a check that reveals whether protected data changed. JWE names the required algorithm in its enc header.

sections.title: Representing Keys as JWKs
sections.content:
A JSON Web Key uses the kty parameter to identify an elliptic-curve key (EC), an RSA key (RSA) or a symmetric key represented as an octet sequence (oct). RSA and octet keys are Required key types; EC is Recommended+.

An EC public key has a curve name in crv and coordinates in x and y. The RFC defines P-256, P-384 and P-521, and coordinates must use the full size required by the curve. An EC private key adds d.

An RSA public key uses n for the modulus and e for the exponent. RSA private keys add d and may include the prime factors and related values. An octet key uses k for its key value.
sections.plainLanguage: A JWK is a JSON object with labeled fields for a cryptographic key. The required fields depend on whether the key is elliptic-curve, RSA or symmetric.

sections.title: Registries for Algorithms and Key Fields
sections.content:
RFC 7518 establishes IANA registries for JWS and JWE algorithms, header parameter names, JWE compression algorithms, JWK key types, JWK parameters and JWK elliptic curves. The initial compression entry is DEF, meaning DEFLATE.

New values use Specification Required review, including a three-week review period and advice from one or more Designated Experts. Experts consider whether a requested value duplicates existing functionality, is generally useful and has a clear description.

The requirement level for an algorithm can change as cryptographic conditions change. New registrations should identify algorithms that remain credible, or mark them Deprecated or Prohibited.
sections.plainLanguage: IANA maintains registries for algorithm names, key types, key fields and curves. Reviewers check that new entries are clear and do not duplicate existing entries.

sections.title: Key Use and Algorithm Security
sections.content:
Implementations should be modular because cryptographic algorithms can become weaker over time. They must protect private and symmetric keys and should limit the key sizes they accept to avoid excessive processing from attacker-supplied values.

An AES GCM key must not be used for more than 2^32 encryption operations, and its IV must never be reused with that key. Unsecured JWS provides no integrity protection, so an application must enable it only for an object where that is acceptable.

The RFC also cautions against reusing the complete set of key material when encrypting keys. PBES2 depends on password strength and iteration count; the specified salt must be random for each encryption, and the RFC recommends at least 1000 iterations.
sections.plainLanguage: Implementations must protect secret keys and should be ready to replace algorithms as needed. They must not reuse an AES GCM IV with the same key or accept unsigned JWS content by default.
